reconcile.connective: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown read the OT refusals as answers to hypocritical, idol-tainted prayer, not to the sincere calling Joel and Paul promise will save.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible sets Joel/Acts/Romans's unconditional 'whosoever' flatly against Matthew, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Micah's refusals, with no harmonizing gloss offered.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/call_on.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: not hear--because their prayers are hypocritical: their hearts are still idolatrous. God never refuses to hear real prayer (Jer 7:21-22; Pro 1:28; Isa 1:15; Isa 58:3).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the harmonizing principle that resolves the whole cluster: the OT refusal texts describe hypocritical/idolatrous cries, not the sincere calling Joel/Acts/Romans promise will be heard.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), "Piety Evinced" (Ethical Discrepancies, p. 231)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley pairs Matthew 7:21 (and Luke 6:46) directly against 1 Corinthians 12:3, ruling that the 'Lord, Lord' of the rejected is 'mere lip-service,' not the 'hearty and spontaneous confession' Paul means -- the same distinguishing move this row's commentators apply to the wider Joel/Acts/Romans-vs-Jeremiah/Ezekiel/Micah cluster.

link.title: What does it mean that "whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13)?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the promise-side texts (Joel/Acts/Romans); argues calling on the Lord is more than verbal utterance, but does not itself cross-reference Matthew 7:21/Jeremiah 14:12/Ezekiel 8:18/Micah 3:4.
